node.label: Stephen Greenblatt
node.description: A literary scholar and theorist whose New Historicism reads literature within the whole field of a period’s culture. Renaissance Self-Fashioning (1980) examines how More, Tyndale, Wyatt, Spenser, Marlowe and Shakespeare fashioned selves, finding that new questions about identity shaped sixteenth-century writing. He calls New Historicism ‘madly eclectic’: it grew from impatience with American formalism and with Marxist criticism, and drew on Foucault to escape the base/superstructure dichotomy, as well as on Walter Benjamin, Michel de Certeau and Clifford Geertz. He credits Raymond Williams with showing how to connect art to the world in which it is made. Sarah Maza questions how far New Historicism and historians’ cultural history actually meet across disciplinary lines, and John Monfasani criticized The Swerve for opposing medieval darkness to Renaissance modernity; Greenblatt replied defending the Renaissance and the importance of atomism.
